turns.prompt:
You are given an attached CSV file b3_supercon_data.csv: 300 real samples,
column `composition` (element fractions as a compact formula string) and
column `target` (the measured critical temperature Tc (K)).

Propose a composition — a value for each element fraction below, within each
observed range, that MAXIMIZES critical temperature Tc (K). Design
variables:
  - O (fraction in [0, 0.697674])
  - Cu (fraction in [0, 0.454545])
  - Ba (fraction in [0, 0.333333])
  - Sr (fraction in [0, 0.285714])
  - Y (fraction in [0, 0.4])
  - Ca (fraction in [0, 0.272727])
  - La (fraction in [0, 0.78])
  - Bi (fraction in [0, 0.521978])
  - Fe (fraction in [0, 0.502513])
  - Nb (fraction in [0, 0.98])
  - C (fraction in [0, 0.972])
  - Pr (fraction in [0, 0.265043])

  - V (fraction in [0, 0.9918])

Reason from the training data, then end with your explicit proposal, e.g.

Ca=0.136364, La=0.39, Bi=0.260989, Fe=0.251256, Nb=0.49, C=0.486,

turns.answer_text:
The highest-\(T_c\) entries that can be realized using only the 20 allowed elements (i.e., that do not require Hg, Tl, H or S) are the Ba-Ca-Cu-O cuprates.  The explicit training point Ba2Ca2Cu3O already reaches 126 K.  Parsing that formula gives the atomic fractions

O = 1/8 = 0.125,  
Cu = 3/8 = 0.375,  
Ba = 2/8 = 0.25,  
Ca = 2/8 = 0.25  

(all well inside the supplied box constraints) and every other listed element equal to zero.  These four values already sum to 1, producing a valid composition.  All other high-\(T_c\) families either need disallowed elements or give substantially lower \(T_c\) once they are restricted to the 20-element set.  Consequently the fractions above are the empirically strongest proposal that can be read off the data.
